doc.title: Artie Shaw — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: After the war: analysis and the last bands
title: Ending analysis, deciding to return, sitting in with Basie and Lester Young
summary: His analyst told him to go back; after nine months off he sat in with Basie in Los Angeles between Lester and Earle Warren and rebuilt his chops.

story.theme_name: Lester Young: the man, the sound, the Basie years
story.community_name: Remembering Lester Young: Prez the man and his sound

blocks.x: You did—obviously after you came back—you continued to progress, because your music changed, didn’t it? Music evolved, yeah?
You’re part of your culture. Either that, or you’re a dinosaur.

The net result was, at the end I said, “I guess I gotta go back now.” She said, “Yeah. Life is first. Analysis is second.” I said, “If I go back, I’ve got nothin’ I can do except have a band.” She said, “Have that.”
How long did you not play the clarinet for?

I didn’t play for about nine months, except now and then, when I’d have to go out . . . no, when I got ready to go out, Basie came to town. I used to sit in with Basie down in Central Avenue. I’d sit between Lester and Earle Warren. That’s when Lester and I got to know each other. Lester liked what I did, and I liked what he did.

Oh, it was very interesting. Sure. As a matter of fact, they put out some records. A couple of pieces. Basie with me playing in them. One of them’s Lady Be Good and a blues. I don’t know what. I never knew it. Somebody played me the record. That’s what I used to do. That was fine. I’d go down there for one night and play. Play what you want.
You kept your chops up, because obviously . . .
That was to build my chops up.
Yeah, build your chops up, because it’s a long layoff.
